1	# HITL Business Pattern Recognition Guide
2	
3	Use this guide to decide whether a business process needs a Human-in-the-Loop node, and where to place it — even when the user has not explicitly asked for one.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## When to Recommend HITL
8	
9	Look for these signals in the business description or process context:
10	
11	### Approval gate
12	The automation produces something that requires sign-off before it can proceed.
13	
14	| Signal phrases | Examples |
15	|---|---|
16	| "approve", "sign off", "authorize", "get approval" | Invoice approval, PO sign-off, budget authorization |
17	| "four-eyes check", "dual control", "maker-checker" | Financial transactions, compliance workflows |
18	| "review before posting", "validate before sending" | CRM updates, email campaigns, database writes |
19	
20	**Insertion point:** After the automation generates the artifact to review, before it takes the action requiring approval.
21	
22	---
23	
24	### Exception escalation
25	The automation hits a case it cannot resolve autonomously and needs a human decision.
26	
27	| Signal phrases | Examples |
28	|---|---|
29	| "if uncertain / low confidence, escalate" | AI agent confidence threshold |
30	| "edge case", "anomaly", "exception handling" | Fraud alerts, out-of-policy transactions |
31	| "escalate to manager / supervisor" | Customer service workflows |
32	
33	**Insertion point:** Inside a conditional branch where the automation detects it cannot proceed alone.
34	
35	---
36	
37	### Data enrichment
38	The automation extracted or generated data that is incomplete — a human must fill in the gaps.
39	
40	| Signal phrases | Examples |
41	|---|---|
42	| "fill in missing fields", "enrich", "complete the record" | Partially extracted invoice data |
43	| "human validates / corrects" | OCR output verification |
44	| "needs human input before continuing" | Missing vendor code, unknown cost center |
45	
46	**Insertion point:** After extraction/generation, before the downstream step that requires complete data.
47	
48	---
49	
50	### Compliance and audit checkpoint
51	A regulation or internal policy requires documented human sign-off.
52	
53	| Signal phrases | Examples |
54	|---|---|
55	| "compliance", "audit trail", "regulatory sign-off" | SOX controls, GDPR consent flows |
56	| "must be reviewed by", "requires attestation" | Legal review gates, privacy impact assessments |
57	
58	**Insertion point:** At the mandated checkpoint defined by the regulation or policy.
59	
60	---
61	
62	### Write-back validation
63	An agent or automation is about to write to an external system — a human must confirm the proposed change.
64	
65	| Signal phrases | Examples |
66	|---|---|
67	| "before writing to", "before posting to", "agent writes to ServiceNow / SAP / CRM" | Any write to a system of record |
68	| "human confirms before agent acts" | Autonomous agent guard rails |
69	
70	**Insertion point:** Immediately before the write/post action.
71	
72	---
73	
74	### Agentic output review
75	An AI agent produced a document, draft, classification, or recommendation — a human must verify it before the result is used or published.
76	
77	| Signal phrases | Examples |
78	|---|---|
79	| "review AI-generated content", "human verifies before sending" | Agent-drafted emails, RCA reports, meeting summaries |
80	| "check before publishing", "validate AI output" | AI-written case notes, support ticket responses |
81	| "human in the loop for AI decisions" | Any LLM output going to a system of record or customer |
82	
83	**Insertion point:** After the agent node, before the downstream action that consumes the output.
84	
85	---
86	
87	### IT / change management approval
88	A change request or access request needs human authorization before the automation executes it.
89	
90	| Signal phrases | Examples |
91	|---|---|
92	| "CAB approval", "change request", "change window" | IT change management (ServiceNow, Jira Service Management) |
93	| "access request", "provision access", "grant permission" | Identity and access management workflows |
94	| "runbook approval", "deployment sign-off" | DevOps release gates |
95	
96	**Insertion point:** After the automation prepares the change record, before it applies the change.
97	
98	---
99	
100	### HR and offer / contract workflows
101	A document or decision with legal or HR significance must be reviewed before it is sent to a third party.
102	
103	| Signal phrases | Examples |
104	|---|---|
105	| "offer letter", "employment contract", "onboarding approval" | HR hiring workflows |
106	| "termination review", "performance decision" | HR case management |
107	| "contract terms", "counter-sign", "legal review gate" | Procurement, vendor onboarding |
108	
109	**Insertion point:** After document generation, before the document is dispatched.
110	
111	---
112	
113	### Customer communication approval
114	An automation is about to send a message on behalf of a person or brand — a human must review tone, accuracy, or content before it goes out.
115	
116	| Signal phrases | Examples |
117	|---|---|
118	| "approve before sending", "review draft email", "check before posting" | Customer support responses, marketing emails |
119	| "agent-written reply", "draft response" | Helpdesk, CRM follow-ups |
120	
121	**Insertion point:** After the draft is generated, before the send/post action.
122	
123	---
124	
125	### Financial transaction approval
126	A monetary action above a threshold or of a certain type requires human sign-off.
127	
128	| Signal phrases | Examples |
129	|---|---|
130	| "above threshold", "over limit", "exceeds budget" | PO approval, expense reimbursement over limit |
131	| "wire transfer", "payment release", "credit note" | AP/AR workflows |
132	| "price override", "discount approval" | Sales quote approval |
133	
134	**Insertion point:** After the automation determines the transaction details, before it submits the payment or posts the entry.
135	
136	---
137	
138	## When NOT to Recommend HITL
139	
140	- The process description is fully automated with no decision point (e.g. "process all invoices automatically")
141	- The human interaction is asynchronous notification only (use email/Slack activity instead)
142	- The user explicitly says no human review is needed
143	- The decision can be made by a rule or AI model with sufficient confidence
144	- The user is asking about **runtime task management** — reassigning, monitoring, cancelling, or checking the status of existing Action Center tasks. These are operational questions answered by `uip tasks` commands or the Orchestrator UI, not by adding a HITL node. A question like "how do I reassign a task sitting for 3 days?" is task administration, not automation authoring — do not recommend adding a HITL checkpoint in response.
145	
146	---
147	
148	## Proactive HITL Recommendation
149	
150	If a business description contains any of the above signals but the user has not asked for a HITL, flag it:
151	
152	> "This process includes [signal]. Before the automation [action], a human should review [data]. I recommend inserting a HITL node here — want me to add it?"
153	
154	Then proceed to Step 3 (schema design) only after the user confirms.
155

1	---
2	name: uipath-human-in-the-loop
3	description: "UiPath Human-in-the-Loop / HITL node authoring — building approval gates, escalations, write-back validation, and data enrichment checkpoints in Flow, Maestro, or Coded Agents. NOT for managing, reassigning, or monitoring tasks at runtime (use uipath-tasks for that)."
4	allowed-tools: Bash, Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep
5	---
6	
7	# UiPath Human-in-the-Loop Assistant
8	
9	Recognizes when a business process needs a human decision point, designs the task schema through conversation, and wires the HITL node into the automation — Flow, Maestro, or Agent.
10	
11	> **Coded agents:** for wiring HITL inside a coded agent, use the `uipath-agents` skill — see `skills/uipath-agents/references/coded/capabilities/human-in-the-loop.md`.
12	
13	## When to Use This Skill
14	
15	- User describes **approval gates** — invoice approval, offer letter review, compliance sign-off, PO authorization
16	- User describes **exception escalation** — "if confidence is low, escalate to a human", fraud alert review
17	- User describes **write-back validation** — "human approves before agent writes to ServiceNow / SAP / CRM"
18	- User describes **data enrichment** — human fills in missing fields the automation cannot resolve
19	- User describes **agentic output review** — "review AI-generated email/RCA/summary before it goes out"
20	- User describes **IT change or access approval** — CAB gate, runbook sign-off, access provisioning review
21	- User describes **HR or contract workflow** — offer letter review, contract approval, termination sign-off
22	- User describes **financial transaction approval** — payment release, price override, expense over limit
23	- User describes **customer communication approval** — agent-drafted reply that needs human sign-off before sending
24	- User explicitly asks to **add a HITL node**, human review step, or Action Center task
25	- User is building any automation where **a human must act before the process can continue**
26	
27	**Do not use this skill for:** managing, reassigning, escalating, or monitoring existing Action Center tasks at runtime — use the `uipath-tasks` skill for those operations. When answering a runtime task management question, provide only administration guidance. Do NOT suggest adding a HITL node, flow, or automation as a follow-up tip or recommendation — even if delays or escalations are mentioned.
28	
29	See [references/hitl-patterns.md](references/hitl-patterns.md) for the full business pattern recognition guide.
30	
31	---
32	
33	## Critical Rules
34	
35	1. **Confirm schema with the user before writing anything for quickform type.** Show the designed schema and wait for explicit confirmation.
36	2. **Always wire the `completed` handle.** A HITL node with no outgoing edge on `completed` blocks the flow forever. Only `completed` is available as an output handle — **not** `output`, `success`, or any other name. This is true even when inserting into an existing flow whose other nodes use `"sourcePort": "output"`.
37	3. **Always add the definition entry when inserting into an existing flow.** Before writing the node, check `workflow.definitions[]` for the correct `nodeType` for the selected path (`"uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form"` for QuickForm, `"uipath.human-in-the-loop.coded-action-app"` for app-based). If absent, append the full definition entry (with `handleConfiguration` including the `completed` handle). Skipping the definition means the `completed` handle is invisible to the runtime and the wiring check fails.
38	4. **Regenerate `variables.nodes` after adding the node.** Replace the entire `workflow.variables.nodes` array — do not append. See the reference docs for the algorithm.
39	5. **Validate after every change.** Run `uip maestro flow validate <file> --output json` after writing the node and edges. The `uip` CLI does not accept `--format`; using it produces `error: unknown option '--format'` and exit code 3.
40	6. **Read the existing `.flow` file before adding.** Understand which nodes already exist and where the HITL checkpoint belongs in the flow.
41	7. **The definition entry is added once per node type.** Check `workflow.definitions` — if an entry with the matching `nodeType` is already there, do not add it again.
42	8. **Check existing node IDs before generating a new one.** Read `workflow.nodes[*].id` from the `.flow` file and pick the next available suffix (e.g. `invoiceReview1`, then `invoiceReview2`).
43	9. **Never report a failed validation as done.** If `uip maestro flow validate` returns errors, diagnose from the JSON output and fix before reporting to the user.
44	10. **Output fields are accessed by `field.id`, not `field.variable`.** The runtime result object uses field IDs as keys — `$vars.<nodeId>.output.<fieldId>`. The `variable` property only creates a workflow-global alias; it does NOT change the key used in the node output object, and it is NOT how downstream scripts read the value.
45	    - WRONG: `$vars.legalApproval` — this is the global alias path, not the script access path
46	    - WRONG: `$vars.<nodeId>.output.legalApproval` — this uses the variable name as the key
47	    - RIGHT: `$vars.<nodeId>.output.approved` — uses `field.id` ("approved") as the key
48	    In every downstream script, use `$vars.<nodeId>.output.<fieldId>` where `<fieldId>` is the `id` you gave the field in the schema — never the `variable` name.
49	11. **Input field binding paths use the upstream output key, not the HITL field's own `id`.** These are two different things: the HITL field `id` identifies the form field (always lowercase); the binding path key is the name used in the upstream script's `return` statement (preserves camelCase). If a script returns `{ supplierName: "Acme" }`, the correct binding is `vars.fetchSupplier.output.supplierName` — writing `suppliername` (the field `id`) produces a path that does not exist at runtime. The form field will be blank; `flow validate` will not catch it. Always derive the binding key from the upstream script source, not from the HITL schema you are designing.
50	12. **Downstream scripts must access `$vars.<nodeId>.output`.** Any script node that runs after the HITL node must read `$vars.<nodeId>.output` (the result object) — do not rely solely on `$vars.<nodeId>.status`. Concrete example: `const output = $vars.reviewNode1.output; const reason = output.reason;`. This is required even when the primary routing uses `status`.
51	
52	---
53	
54	## Step 0 — Resolve the `uip` binary
55	
56	```bash
57	UIP=$(command -v uip 2>/dev/null || npm root -g 2>/dev/null | sed 's|/node_modules$||')/bin/uip
58	$UIP --version
59	```
60	
61	Use `$UIP` in place of `uip` for all subsequent commands if the plain `uip` command isn't found.
62	
63	> **Local dev note:** If working inside the uipcli repo, replace `uip` with `bun run start`.
64	
65	---
66	
67	## Step 1 — Detect the Surface and Find the Flow File
68	
69	Run these checks in order:
70	
71	```bash
72	# Check for a .flow file (Flow project)
73	find . -name "*.flow" -maxdepth 4 | head -5
74	
75	# Check for agent.json (Low-Code Agent project)
76	find . -name "agent.json" -maxdepth 4 | head -3
77	
78	# Check for Maestro .bpmn (Maestro process)
79	find . -name "*.bpmn" -maxdepth 4 | head -3
80	```
81	
82	| Found | Surface | How HITL is added |
83	|---|---|---|
84	| `.flow` file | **Flow** | Write node JSON directly — see reference docs |
85	| `agent.json` | **Low Code Agent** | Escalation CLI in-flight — guide manually for now |
86	| `.bpmn` (Maestro) | **Maestro** | Not yet — guide user manually |
87	
88	**If the user mentioned a specific file path**, use that directly.
89	
90	**If no `.flow` file exists and surface is Flow**, scaffold solution-first — Flow projects MUST live inside a solution:
91	
92	```bash
93	# Probe the solution verb once per session before scaffolding:
94	#   uip solution init --help --output json
95	# Success → use `solution init` (post-rename, default).
96	# `unknown command` → CLI predates the rename; substitute `uip solution new <SolutionName>` below.
97	
98	uip solution init <SolutionName> --output json
99	cd <SolutionName> && uip maestro flow init <ProjectName>
100	# Creates: <SolutionName>/<ProjectName>/<ProjectName>.flow
101	```
102	
103	The flow file path is `<SolutionName>/<ProjectName>/<ProjectName>.flow` (double-nested). `<SolutionName>/` is the solution directory (contains the `.uipx` file); `<ProjectName>/` inside it is the flow project. By convention `<SolutionName>` and `<ProjectName>` are often the same string, but they are two distinct scaffolding arguments. Running `uip maestro flow init` without first running `uip solution init` produces a broken single-nested `<ProjectName>/<ProjectName>.flow` layout that fails Studio Web upload, packaging, and downstream tooling.
104	
105	---
106	
107	## Step 2 — Read the Business Context
108	
109	Read the existing `.flow` file to understand current nodes and edges. Use the Read tool on the `.flow` file path, then identify:
110	1. **Where** the human decision point belongs (after which existing node)
111	2. **What the human needs to see** — data produced by upstream nodes
112	3. **What the human must provide back** — data needed by downstream nodes
113	4. **What actions they can take** — the named outcome buttons
114	5. **Form type**: QuickForm (inline schema, node type `uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form`) or AppTask (deployed coded app, node type `uipath.human-in-the-loop.coded-action-app`)?
115	
116	---
117	
118	## Step 2b — Proactive HITL Recommendation
119	
120	**If the user did NOT explicitly mention HITL**, scan the business description for these signals before proceeding:
121	
122	| Signal | Pattern | Why a human checkpoint matters |
123	|---|---|---|
124	| "agent writes to", "updates", "posts to" an external system | Write-back validation | Prevents incorrect writes to production systems |
125	| "if confidence is low", "when uncertain", "edge case" | Exception escalation | Agent cannot resolve autonomously |
126	| "approves", "reviews", "signs off", "four-eyes" | Approval gate | Business or compliance requirement |
127	| "fills in missing", "validates extraction", "corrects" | Data enrichment | Automation produced incomplete data |
128	| "compliance", "regulatory", "audit trail" | Compliance checkpoint | Mandated human sign-off |
129	
130	**When a signal is found, say this before doing anything else:**
131	
132	> "I noticed that [quote the specific part of their description]. This is a [pattern name] — a point where [brief consequence if no human reviews]. I recommend inserting a Human-in-the-Loop step here so that [human role] can [action] before the automation [continues/writes/sends]. Should I add it?"
133	
134	Wait for confirmation. Do not proceed to schema design until the user confirms.
135	
136	**Example:**
137	> User: "Build an automation that reads support tickets, uses AI to generate an RCA, and updates the ticket in ServiceNow."
138	>
139	> Agent: "I noticed that the automation writes AI-generated content directly back to ServiceNow. This is a write-back validation pattern — if the RCA is incorrect and nobody reviews it, wrong data goes into production tickets. I recommend inserting a Human-in-the-Loop step so that a support lead can review and optionally edit the RCA before the update is applied. Should I add it?"
140	
141	---
142	
143	## Step 3 — Choose Task Type
144	
145	Present the user with three options. Do not choose on their behalf or perform any registry search.
146	
147	| # | Option | Node type | Description |
148	|---|---|---|---|
149	| 1 | **QuickForm** | `uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form` | Inline typed form — fields rendered by Action Center from the schema you design here |
150	| 2 | **New Coded Action App** | `uipath.human-in-the-loop.coded-action-app` | Scaffold a new React + TypeScript app inside the solution — full UI control |
151	| 3 | **Existing Deployed App** | `uipath.human-in-the-loop.coded-action-app` | Reference an app already deployed to Orchestrator |
152	
153	> **If the user's request is purely business-oriented** (no mention of a deployed app, coded action app, or custom UI): skip the question and proceed directly with QuickForm. Do not ask. Say: "I'll use QuickForm — it's inline, no deployment step needed, and works for most approval and review tasks."
154	
155	> **If the user is unsure or says "just pick one":** Default to QuickForm. Say: "I'll use QuickForm — it's the quickest to set up and works for most approval and review tasks. You can always upgrade to a Coded Action App later."
156	
157	| User selects | Next step |
158	|---|---|
159	| QuickForm | Read [How to write a QuickForm HITL node](references/hitl-node-quickform.md) for Steps 1–2, then continue with Step 4 |
160	| New Coded Action App | Read [How to scaffold a new Coded Action App](references/hitl-node-coded-action-app.md) for Step 4c details, then continue with Step 4 |
161	| Existing Deployed App → ask: "What is the name of the deployed action app?" | Read [How to wire an existing deployed Action App](references/hitl-node-apptask.md) for Step 4b details, then continue with Step 4 |
162	
163	**Fallback rules — what to do when the chosen path hits a blocker:**
164	
165	| Path | Blocker | Response |
166	|---|---|---|
167	| Existing Deployed App | App not found in Orchestrator | "I couldn't find an app with that name. Would you like to try a different name, or fall back to QuickForm while you prepare the app?" |
168	| New Coded Action App | No `dist/` build present in the source path | "The source folder doesn't have a `dist/` build yet. Run your build first (`npm run build` or equivalent), then come back. Or I can set up a QuickForm now so the flow is wired and ready — you can swap in the app later." |
169	| New Coded Action App | User can't provide a source path | "If you don't have the app code ready yet, I'll use QuickForm to wire the HITL checkpoint. You can replace it with a Coded Action App once it's built." |
170	| Any custom app | Auth expired (401 on API call) | "The session looks expired — run `uip login` to refresh your credentials, then retry." |
171	
172	---
173	
174	## Step 4 — Common configuration
175	
176	| Timeout | "How long before the task times out if nobody acts? (default: 24 hours)" |
177	| Priority | "What priority should this task have? Options: Low, Medium, High (default: Low)" |
178	
179	---
180	
181	## Step 4b — Schema Design Rules (QuickForm only)
182	
183	Apply these rules unconditionally while designing the schema.
184	
185	### Field direction
186	
187	Pick direction based on what the human does with the field:
188	
189	| Signal | Direction |
190	|---|---|
191	| "can see", "shown to", "read-only", "displays", "context for reviewer" | `input` |
192	| "fills in", "enters", "types", "selects", "required decision", "approves" | `output` |
193	| "can edit", "can correct", "pre-filled but editable", "suggested value the reviewer can adjust" | `inOut` |
194	
195	`inOut` means the field is pre-populated from an upstream node AND the human can modify it before submitting. The runtime exposes it under `$vars.<nodeId>.output.<fieldId>` the same as an output field.
196	
197	### Field types
198	
199	Use the JS/JSON type that fits the field: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `date`, or `file`. These are the only valid values — do not use `text`.
200	
201	### Vague or incomplete schema descriptions
202	
203	If the user says something like "just add some fields" or "use whatever makes sense":
204	
205	1. Infer sensible defaults from the upstream data and downstream needs visible in the `.flow` file.
206	2. If there are no upstream nodes to bind to (flow is just a trigger), use output-direction fields only.
207	
208	### Empty field labels block validation
209	
210	Every field in `inputs.schema.fields` must have a non-empty `label`. `flow validate` emits `HITL_QUICK_FORM_FIELD_LABEL_REQUIRED` (error severity) for each field with an empty or whitespace-only `label` — Debug and Publish are blocked until all labels are filled in. Never generate a field with `"label": ""` or omit the `label` key.

214	## Step 5 — Write the Node Directly
215	
216	### Surface: Flow — QuickForm (inline schema only)
217	
218	Write the node JSON directly into `workflow.nodes`, add the definition to `workflow.definitions` (once), wire edges into `workflow.edges`, and regenerate `workflow.variables.nodes`. **Direct JSON is the default.**
219	
220	Node JSON, definition entry, edge format, `variables.nodes` algorithm, and four worked examples: **[How to write a QuickForm HITL node](references/hitl-node-quickform.md)**
221	
222	**CLI (opt-in):** When the user explicitly requests a CLI command:
223	
224	```bash
225	uip maestro flow hitl add <path/to/file.flow> \
226	  --label "<TaskLabel>" \
227	  --priority <Low|Medium|High> \
228	  --assignee <email-or-group> \
229	  --schema '<json>' \
230	  --output json
231	```
232	
233	The CLI writes the node, adds the definition entry, and updates `variables.nodes` automatically. Wire the `completed` port after it returns.
234

239	```

242

251	```bash

253	```

256	
257	Step 4b must be completed first — app resolved, configuration retrieved. Then:
258	
259	Resolve the solution context (`.uipx` file), write solution resource files, register the app reference, merge `debug_overwrites.json`, then write the node JSON (type `uipath.human-in-the-loop.coded-action-app`) with `inputs.app` populated from the Step 3b configuration.

261	App search/selection, retrieve-configuration, resource file writing, complete node JSON with `appInputBindings`: **[How to wire an existing deployed Action App](references/hitl-node-apptask.md)**

265	```bash

267	```

270

276	  "escalations": [
277	    {
278	      "name": "<escalation-name>",
279	      "inputSchema":  { "inputs": [...], "inOuts": [...] },

292	    data={ "fieldName": value }
293	))

298	
299	The Maestro HITL CLI is not yet available. Guide the user to add the HITL node manually in the Maestro process designer using the schema from Step 5. In Maestro, field names in `outputs`/`inOuts` must exactly match declared process variable names and types.
